query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The intrinsic chemical complexity of iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles leads to local compositional fluctuations that cause a broadened, multi‐step premelting and melting transition, in contrast to the sharp, singular melting behavior observed in chemically uniform, single‐metal nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu) synthesized to form a single, solid solution phase with controlled particle sizes (e.g., 5–20 nm)
generation.intervention: Subject both the HEA nanoparticles and baseline single-metal nanoparticles to identical heating/cooling thermal ramp protocols across the premelting and melting regime using techniques such as in situ TEM and DSC
generation.conditions: Identical nanoparticle size distributions, identical thermal ramp rates (capturing temperature changes from well below the premelting regime to full melting), and controlled atmospheres to minimize extraneous thermal effects
generation.structural_mediator: Local elemental heterogeneity within the HEA nanoparticles
generation.mechanism: Due to the presence of multiple elements with differing individual melting characteristics and limited atomic mobility, spatial compositional fluctuations cause a distribution of local melting temperatures. This leads to a gradual, multi‐step phase transition during premelting and melting, as opposed to the uniform, sharp melting transition seen with single-metal nanoparticles.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a broadened melting range with multiple steps or inflection points in the DSC curve and observable phase-coexistence regions during in situ TEM heating, whereas baseline single-metal nanoparticles will display a sharp, singular melting point.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles composed of a single metal (or chemically uniform nanoparticles) subjected to the same thermal treatment, which are expected to have a narrow, singular melting transition
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to apply under rapid thermal annealing conditions (as in pulsed heating/cooling protocols) and for particles in the nanoscale regime (approximately 5–20 nm), where the effect of local compositional variation is maximized. Outside of these conditions (e.g., bulk materials or extremely slow thermal ramps) other mechanisms may dominate the melting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of transition broadening and the number of observable melting steps may vary with nanoparticle size, degree of compositional inhomogeneity, and interatomic interactions, making precise quantification uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: (a) iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles and (b) monometallic nanoparticles (e.g., pure iron or another representative single metal) with matched size distributions. Subject both sets to identical in situ TEM thermal ramping and DSC measurements across the premelting to melting regime.
measurements: DSC curves to determine the onset, peak temperatures, and breadth of melting transitions
In situ TEM imaging to observe structural changes and phase coexistence during heating
Mapping of local compositional variations if possible via energy dispersive spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles display a melting behavior similar to the single-metal nanoparticles (i.e., a sharp, singular melting transition with no significant broadening or multi-step features), then the hypothesis that local elemental heterogeneity broadens the phase transition would be falsified.

This behavior contrasts with the bimetallic case, suggesting that the rules governing phase formation differ for the systems containing two or five elements: Single-phase alloy formation occurs more readily if more elements are present, as systems that are immiscible on the bimetallic level can be driven to mix by introducing more elements. As the resulting phases of the binary particles cannot readily be explained by their thermodynamic stability, we devised a kinetic model to rationalize the experimental results based on the restrictions imposed by the synthesis. When comparing five-element and two-element mixtures, the concentration of individual atom types is reduced the more elements are present. This will make it increasingly difficult for elements with strong preferences of ordering to form an intermetallic structure or for elements that repulse each other to segregate, simply because they are more dilute. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. occupying_moves.technique: in‐situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with rapid thermal annealing
occupying_moves.conditions: nanoparticles examined continuously from well below premelting to full melting; controlling and measuring the temperature ramp to capture the onset and consolidation of the solid solution during cooling

occupying_moves.technique: comparative differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and high‐resolution TEM
occupying_moves.conditions: side‐by-side tests on high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles versus baseline single‐metal nanoparticles, under identical size distributions and temperature ramp protocols in the premelting/melting window

occupying_moves.technique: molecular dynamics simulations employing realistic interatomic potentials
occupying_moves.conditions: simulations run over a range of nanoparticle sizes and compositions to resolve spatial fluctuations in local cohesion and melting behavior across the premelting to melting regime

chosen.conditions: nanoparticles of controlled size (e.g., 5–20 nm) subjected to identical heating/cooling protocols across the premelting and melting regime, with baseline single‐metal nanoparticles measured in parallel
chosen.why: This move directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that the premelting and melting behavior in high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the intrinsic chemical complexity—namely, that local elemental heterogeneity yields a broader, multi‐step phase transition (compared to the sharp transitions in single‐metal systems). Prior work on bimetallic particles has shown that increased chemical complexity produces varied configurations, so a controlled comparison with single‐metal nanoparticles will decisively reveal whether the broadening of the transition (or any unexpected shift in melting onset) evidences a mechanism based on local compositional fluctuations. An observation that the high‐entropy nanoparticles exhibit the same sharp, singular melting point as the baseline would decisively falsify this hypothesis.
